cards.b:
Infectious disease has shaped history: the Black Death, smallpox, the 1918 flu and COVID-19. Public health, meaning clean water, vaccines and surveillance, has saved more lives than most drugs. This lesson ties microbes, immunity and society together.

The Black Death of the 1300s killed perhaps a third of Europe, and the 1918 influenza killed an estimated 50 million people worldwide, many in India. Disease patterns follow cities, trade and travel. Public health works by prevention: sanitation, clean water, vaccination, nutrition and tracking cases. When John Snow removed the handle of a Broad Street pump in London in 1854, cholera cases dropped, a founding example of epidemiology.

Infectious: caused by germs and can spread (cholera, TB, malaria). Non-communicable: not spread, such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer. Deficiency and genetic diseases form other groups. Disease spreads through air, water, food, vectors (mosquitoes), blood or contact.

Think of an endemic disease as always present in a region (malaria in some districts), an epidemic as a sudden rise above normal, and a pandemic as one that spreads across continents. Spread routes matter for control: airborne diseases need masks and ventilation, waterborne diseases need clean water and sanitation, and vector-borne diseases need mosquito control. A carrier can pass on an infection without showing symptoms, as Typhoid Mary did in the early 1900s. Non-communicable diseases now cause most deaths in India.

• Endemic: steady in a region (malaria in some districts).
  • Epidemic: sudden rise in a place.
  • Pandemic: spread across the world (1918 flu, COVID-19, declared March 2020).

R0 is how many people one case infects on average. Above 1, the outbreak grows; below 1, it fades. Control tools: vaccination, isolation, masks, clean water, vector control, contact tracing. John Snow (1854) traced cholera in London to the Broad Street pump, the start of epidemiology.

• Malaria: Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles. Ronald Ross showed this in 1897 in India (Secunderabad).
  • TB: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, airborne.
  • HIV/AIDS: virus attacks helper T cells.
  • Dengue, chikungunya: Aedes mosquitoes.
  • Cholera, typhoid: contaminated water.

Malaria is caused by a single-celled parasite, which infects the liver and then red blood cells, causing cycles of fever. Ronald Ross, working at the Presidency General Hospital in Secunderabad, found the parasite in a mosquito's stomach in 1897 and won the 1902 Nobel Prize. TB is treated with a long course of several antibiotics, and stopping early encourages drug-resistant strains. Dengue spreads in cities because Aedes breeds in clean, stored water such as in coolers and old tyres, so emptying containers weekly helps.

Many new diseases jump from animals: Ebola, SARS, MERS, COVID-19, Nipah, avian flu. Habitat loss and wildlife trade raise the chance. The 'One Health' idea links human, animal and environmental health.

A zoonosis is a disease passing from animals to humans, and about three-fifths of known human infections originate in animals. Nipah virus, carried by fruit bats, caused outbreaks in Kerala in 2018 and later. Rabies, mostly from dog bites, kills thousands in India each year, but can be prevented by vaccination of dogs and prompt post-bite treatment. Because people, animals and environment are linked, One Health teams include doctors, vets and ecologists who share data and plans.

Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, the first human disease wiped out. Polio is nearly gone. Rinderpest in cattle was eradicated in 2011. Wuchereria and Guinea worm are close to elimination. mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 were developed within a year (Karikó and Weissman, Nobel 2023).

Fix these

  • Pandemic means wide spread, not severity.
  • Not all disease is caused by germs.
  • Vaccines and hygiene, not just drugs, are the main tools.

Also, how bad an outbreak is depends on three things: how easily it spreads, how severe it is and how well people are protected. Public health measures such as hand washing, clean water, vaccination and contact tracing work together, and the eradication of smallpox in 1980 and the near-elimination of polio (India was declared polio-free in 2014) show the power of this approach.

Also, handwashing and clean water are public health tools too.

The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme tackles malaria and dengue. The TB programme (now NTEP) offers free DOTS treatment. India eliminated Guinea worm (2000) and trachoma as a public health problem (2024), and was declared maternal and neonatal tetanus free in 2015. Ayushman Bharat (2018) provides health insurance, and the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (2004) tracks outbreaks. ICMR's National Institute of Virology in Pune isolated the first SARS-CoV-2 strain in India in 2020. Malaria deaths fell sharply since 2000.

• Infectious versus non-communicable diseases.
  • Endemic, epidemic, pandemic.
  • R below 1 ends an outbreak.
  • Zoonoses are a rising threat; One Health is the answer.

Think about it:

  1. Why did smallpox eradication succeed but measles has not yet?
  2. How would you decide when to close schools in an outbreak?
